meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Understand It Brings You Luck, Whether You Believe in It or Not'?
meta.ogDescription: The horseshoe story is a Niels Bohr anecdote — and even Bohr is unverified. Einstein does not appear in it for thirty years.

answer.label: Not Einstein — a Niels Bohr anecdote
answer.authorDates: 1885–1962 · Danish theoretical physicist · Nobel Prize in Physics, 1922
answer.sourceLine: For its first thirty years, every documented telling of the horseshoe story that names anyone at all names the Danish physicist Niels Bohr — beginning with the earliest known printing, Stockholm’s Svenska Dagbladet of 4 January 1956 — while two retellings, in 1959 and 1973, leave the physicist unnamed. Einstein does not enter the story until a Washington Post column of 26 June 1986, whose author already hedged it as “perhaps apocryphal, perhaps not” — and Quote Investigator ↗ found no direct evidence for the remark in Bohr’s own writings either, so this is a Bohr anecdote rather than a documented Bohr quotation.

source.heading: The earliest documented telling

docMeta.dd: 4 January 1956, Stockholm — quote page 8, column 6; article headed “Det påstås”

Swedish original; the English rendering is Quote Investigator’s. The earliest English printing verified on paper is The American Weekly, 30 September 1956 — an earlier 1956 English sighting, in Shipbuilding & Shipping Record, is unverified
Not documented until The Washington Post, 26 June 1986, page A24 — thirty years later

source.excerpt: “Niels, it can’t possibly be that you, a brilliant scientist, believe that foolish horseshoe superstition!” — “Of course not,” replied the scientist. “But I understand it’s lucky whether you believe in it or not.”
trail: The earliest match located by Quote Investigator ↗ is an item in Stockholm’s Svenska Dagbladet of 4 January 1956, verified from scans, in which a curious American visitor asks Niels Bohr about the horseshoe above his door.

Through 1956 and 1957 the story spread in English — a syndicated humour column in The American Weekly, Maxwell Droke’s The Speaker’s Handbook of Humor, and the newspaper column “Office Cat” — and, as QI’s chronology ↗ shows, every one of them named Bohr.

Later tellings destabilise the attribution rather than confirm it: Wikiquote ↗ places the line under Disputed and records versions in which Bohr is the questioner, or is merely repeating a story about a neighbour in Tisvilde.
Albert Einstein enters only in 1986, in a Washington Post column that moves the horseshoe to Princeton and flags the tale as possibly apocryphal — the ninth and last citation in QI’s sequence ↗.
source.cutTag: “The Wit Parade” by E. E. Kenyon · 30 September 1956
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest English printing verified on paper (Quote Investigator lists one earlier 1956 English sighting, in Shipbuilding & Shipping Record, that it expressly could not verify), and the closest period wording to the line as it circulates today — but note that it is not identical to it. The familiar form (“I understand it brings you luck, whether you believe in it or not”) matches no transcribed source exactly; it is a smoothed, composite version of wordings that differ in every telling. The earliest printing of all is the Swedish item of 4 January 1956, whose sense runs closer to “a horseshoe can bring good luck even to people who are not superstitious.”
source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for this wording, because no work of established authorship contains it. Every documented telling is from 1956 or later — well past the 1931 line that would make a work public domain in the United States — and each of those printings (a Swedish newspaper item, a syndicated humour column, a 1956 Harper & Brothers anthology) carries its own separate rights in its own particular phrasing. The popular form quoted here matches none of them exactly and has no identifiable author, so quotle.info makes no public-domain claim for it.

author.name: Niels Bohr
author.heading: Who the anecdote is actually told about
author.metaLine: 1885–1962 · Danish theoretical physicist · Nobel Prize in Physics, 1922
author.bio: Niels Bohr (born Copenhagen, 7 October 1885; died there 18 November 1962) was the Danish theoretical physicist who gave quantum theory its first working picture of the atom, and who spent the rest of his life arguing about what that picture meant — most famously with Einstein. He took the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on atomic structure and the radiation atoms emit. He also attracted stories: colleagues and biographers recorded a steady stream of Bohr sayings, and this is one of several that circulate widely without ever surfacing in anything he actually wrote.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented telling: “Det påstås,” Svenska Dagbladet (Stockholm), 4 January 1956, quote page 8, column 6 — naming Niels Bohr. Earliest English printing verified on paper: E. E. Kenyon, “The Wit Parade,” The American Weekly, in the Cleveland Plain Dealer, 30 September 1956, quote page 13, column 1. The attribution to Albert Einstein is not documented until Joseph Laitin, “A Rare Media Leak,” The Washington Post, 26 June 1986, page A24. Chronology per Quote Investigator ↗; no primary source in either man’s own writings has been located.

copyAttribution: Not Albert Einstein. The horseshoe anecdote — "Of course I don't believe in it, but I understand it brings you luck, whether you believe in it or not." — is told of the Danish physicist Niels Bohr in every documented version that names anyone at all, from its earliest known printing (Svenska Dagbladet, Stockholm, 4 January 1956) onward; two retellings, in 1959 and 1973, leave the physicist unnamed. Einstein does not appear in the story until a Washington Post column of 26 June 1986, whose author called it "perhaps apocryphal, perhaps not." Quote Investigator found no direct evidence for the remark in Bohr's own writings either, and Wikiquote lists it under Disputed — so it is a Bohr anecdote, not a sourced Bohr quotation. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it keeps moving
misattribution.intro: This is a travelling anecdote, not a quotation with a home. It has been pinned on at least three physicists and one psychiatrist’s unnamed host, and the paper trail lets you watch it move.

items.why: Einstein appears in no documented telling until Quote Investigator’s ↗ ninth citation: Joseph Laitin’s column in The Washington Post of 26 June 1986, which relocates the horseshoe to a Princeton front door. Laitin himself introduced it as a story “perhaps apocryphal, perhaps not.” The anecdote does not appear anywhere on Einstein’s Wikiquote page ↗ — not even among the misattributions.

items.scope: The earliest and most persistent credit
items.why: Bohr is named in the 4 January 1956 Svenska Dagbladet item and in every English printing that follows through the 1950s and 1970s. But QI ↗ located no direct evidence in Bohr’s own writings, and Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Disputed. This is the best-supported name on the story, not a sourced quotation from it.

items.scope: The versions with no name at all
items.why: Carl Alfred Meier’s 1959 lecture version has him visiting an unidentified “world-famous scientist”; the 1973 anthology A Random Walk in Science gives an unnamed physicist with a horseshoe on a laboratory door, and routes the tale from I. B. Cohen to Samuel Goudsmit to Bohr — making Bohr the audience, not the speaker. Both are catalogued by Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ appends the note “Possibly originated by Samuel Goudsmit” to the entry. That is a suggestion rather than a finding, and no source cited here documents Goudsmit as the author of the line.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: the horseshoe story belongs to Niels Bohr, not Albert Einstein — but it belongs to him as folklore. Its earliest printing is dated 4 January 1956, its Einstein version does not appear for another thirty years, and Quote Investigator ↗ closes with the observation that the origin and veracity of the narrative still await clarifying evidence.

context.heading: Why the horseshoe migrated to Einstein
lead: The joke needs a very specific kind of person to land: someone whose scientific authority is so complete that a folk charm over his door reads as a scandal. For thirty years that person was Niels Bohr — the man who told the world atoms obey rules nobody’s intuition would have guessed. When the story surfaced again in a 1986 Washington Post column, the doorway had moved to Princeton and the physicist had become Einstein, who by then had inherited the role of the world’s default genius.

That is the whole mechanism behind a great many Einstein quotations. The line does not need to sound like him; it needs to need somebody like him, and he is the nearest name at hand. Here the drift is unusually easy to see, because the Bohr paper trail is dense, dated and continuous, and the Einstein version arrives from nowhere three decades in.
context.detailsSummary: The wrinkle: even the Bohr version keeps sliding off Bohr
detailsBody: The tellings do not agree on who owned the horseshoe. In the 1959 lectures of the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Alfred Meier the physicist is simply an unnamed “world-famous scientist”; in the 1973 anthology A Random Walk in Science the horseshoe hangs on a laboratory door and Bohr is explicitly not a participant — the note there routes the tale from the Harvard historian I. B. Cohen to Samuel Goudsmit, who told it to Bohr, “whose favourite story it became.” A 1974 telling puts the horseshoe on Bohr’s country cabin. All of this is set out on Quote Investigator ↗.

Wikiquote ↗ files the remark under its Disputed heading for the same reason, and notes the same instability: it cites Abraham Pais’s Inward Bound for the version in which Bohr answers a visitor at his home in Tisvilde, Samuel Sambursky’s 1974 book for an early version in which Bohr is the one asking and a friend gives the reply, and Heisenberg’s memoir Physics and Beyond for a version in which Bohr is merely repeating a story about a Tisvilde neighbour. Wikiquote adds that the line was “possibly originated by Samuel Goudsmit.”

Quote Investigator also flags a further 1956 sighting in the trade journal Shipbuilding & Shipping Record, crediting the Danish publication “Danmarksposten” — which would suggest the story was already circulating in Denmark. QI states plainly that this entry has not been verified on paper and may be inaccurate, so it is offered here with the same caveat.
context.pull: Einstein does not appear anywhere in this story for thirty years.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Albert Einstein. The earliest tellings name Niels Bohr, but no primary source has been located in his writings and Wikiquote files the line under Disputed — treat it as a Bohr anecdote, not a sourced Bohr quotation. The text quoted here is the earliest paper-verified English printing (The American Weekly, 30 September 1956); the familiar wording matches no transcribed source exactly.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest known match is Svenska Dagbladet, 4 January 1956, quote page 8 column 6, naming Niels Bohr; English printings followed in Sept 1956 (The American Weekly, 'The Wit Parade' by E. E. Kenyon), 1956 (Droke, The Speaker's Handbook of Humor, p.373), Feb 1957 ('Office Cat'), 1959 (Meier, unnamed scientist), 1973 (A Random Walk in Science, unnamed physicist, Cohen→Goudsmit→Bohr), 1974 (Hawkins) and 1986 (Washington Post, 26 June, 'A Rare Media Leak' by Joseph Laitin, p.A24, featuring Albert Einstein and flagged 'perhaps apocryphal, perhaps not'). QI concludes the earliest instances all named Bohr and that it located no direct evidence in Bohr's writings. QI also notes a Shipbuilding & Shipping Record 1956 sighting credited to 'Danmarksposten', expressly not verified on paper.

Wikiquote's Niels Bohr page carries the horseshoe reply ('Of course not ... but I am told it works even if you don't believe in it') under its 'Disputed' section heading, citing Abraham Pais's Inward Bound (1986) p.210, Samuel Sambursky's The Interaction Between Science and Philosophy (1974) p.357 for a version in which a friend gives the reply, and Heisenberg's Physics and Beyond p.92 for a version in which Bohr recounts it about a neighbour in Tisvilde; it adds 'Possibly originated by Samuel Goudsmit.'

Wikiquote's Albert Einstein page does not contain the horseshoe anecdote anywhere — the word 'horseshoe' does not appear on the page, in the sourced quotes, the Disputed section or the Misattributed section.

Niels Bohr was born 7 October 1885 in Copenhagen and died there 18 November 1962; he was a Danish theoretical physicist and won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his investigation of the structure of atoms and the radiation emanating from them.
Albert Einstein was born 14 March 1879 and died 18 April 1955 in Princeton, New Jersey; he joined the Institute for Advanced Study in 1933.

This Internet Archive item is Werner Heisenberg's memoir 'Physics and beyond: encounters and conversations', published by Harper & Row, New York, a translation of Der Teil und das Ganze — the work Wikiquote cites for Bohr retelling the horseshoe story about a Tisvilde neighbour.
